newsitem.title: USA: Amazon.com to go public as rivalry grows.
newsitem.headline: Amazon.com to go public as rivalry grows.

text.p: Internet bookseller Amazon.com Inc. is poised to go public in one of the year's most closely watched stock offerings as its giant rival Barnes & Noble Inc. cranks up the competitive pressure.

Underwriters for the two-year-old Seattle company are expected to price the initial public offering this week and the stock should begin trading on Nasdaq despite a last-minute lawsuit filed by Barnes & Noble.
The lawsuit, filed late on Monday, seeks to block Amazon.com from calling itself "The World's Largest Bookstore," a claim Barnes & Noble calls "false and misleading."

"Amazon is not a bookstore at all," Barnes & Noble complains in its lawsuit, filed in Federal court in New York. "Rather, it is a book broker making use of the Internet exclusively to generate sales to the public."
Amazon.com declined to comment, citing rules governing its statements near the time of its planned stock offering.
Meanwhile Barnes & Noble launched its own Web site Tuesday, boasting more than 1 million available books, the vast majority of which were being offered at prices that undercut Amazon's.

"I think that Barnes & Noble wants to send a strong message, even a shot across the bow at Amazon.com, to show they plan to be major players in online bookselling," said Adam Schoenfeld, analyst at Jupiter Communications.

At first blush, the fight hardly appears to be a fair one, pitting the 124-year-old chain, with more than 1,000 stores and $2.45 billion in sales last year, against a virtual rival that sold $15.7 million worth of books last year from its headquarters in a slightly run-down Seattle office building.

Amazon.com sales are rising exponentially -- the company posted $16 million in sales in the first quarter alone -- but the company warned in its prospectus that such growth rates are probably "not sustainable" and it expects to incur "substantial operating losses for the foreseeable future."
The company lost about $3 million in the first quarter and $6 million last year.
Nevertheless, the Amazon.com offering has been one of the year's hottest, especially since technology stocks have rebounded this month after slumping earlier in the year.

Kathleen Smith, a portfolio manager at Renaissance Capital, said the proposed offering price for the shares apparently has risen to $14 to $16, up from $12 to $14, reflecting strong demand. Underwriters now are expected to sell 3 million shares, up from 2.5 million.
"It's a good company, one of the better names," she said. "There is competition, but there's going to be a lot of room for online booksellers. It's really the wave of the future."

Investors are betting that with a cash infusion of some $40 million, Amazon.com founder Jeff Bezos, 33, will be able to capitalise on the buzz that has made his company one of the best-known names in Internet commerce.
"They're a terrific company -- very dynamic and entrepreneurial," said Schoenfeld. "I expect the IPO to do well. This is going to be a long, nasty fight."

But Amazon.com could have a tough time beating back Barnes & Noble and other rivals. Other booksellers also are dipping in to online waters, including Borders Group Inc., which is expected to announce its Internet plans soon.

"If Barnes & Noble can translate the experience that you have in their physical stores onto the Internet, they can definitely take a lot of customers away from Amazon.com," said Erina DuBois of Dataquest.
She noted that Barnes & Noble already has a more recognisable brand name and tighter relations with book distributors, publishers and authors than Amazon.com.
"They're taking this pretty seriously," she said.
Schoenfeld agreed, saying Barnes & Noble would aggressively defend its "brick and mortar" franchise position in the nation's $21 billion book industry.
